headlines.article_text: Anthropic stock sinks below $83 IPO price Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Anthropic stock sank on Tuesday, falling below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price. Shares of ANT have been dropping steadily since the stock opened at $111.50 on the Nasdaq. Analysts are still bullish about the company, citing its potential to capture a large addressable market. In this article ANT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei inside the Nasdaq MarketSite ahead of the anticipated IPO of artificial intelligence company Anthropic in New York City on November 19, 2026. Charly Triballeau | Afp | Getty Images Shares of Anthropic fell 8% on Tuesday, sending the stock below the artificial intelligence company's $83 IPO price. The AI lab's stock has been sinking steadily since opening at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, after Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest offering of all time. Investors eagerly awaited Anthropic's debut in hopes that the company would revitalize the broader AI trade, which has been volatile in recent weeks over concerns about the feasibility of a multitrillion-dollar infrastructure buildout. Anthropic's initial public offering was oversubscribed, and roughly half of the institutional investors that placed orders for the stock were left empty-handed, as CNBC previously reported . But at least for now, as the market wavers, those firms don't appear to be racing to scoop up shares. Chip stocks Nvidia , Advanced Micro Devices and Intel , as well as neoclouds CoreWeave , IREN and Nebius , all fell during intraday trading on Tuesday. The market is still reeling after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, a dramatic reversal from his ouster earlier this month. Nvidia shares surged more than 30% on Monday, but pared those gains Tuesday. Analysts at Canaccord Genuity said Tuesday that they're focused on Anthropic's long-term potential. They said they believe that the company is building "one of the most important enterprise technology franchises of the AI era" and that the "opportunity is considerably larger than traditional software spending." Canaccord Genuity initiated coverage of Anthropic with a buy rating and a $135 price target. "The risks are unusually large, particularly around infrastructure commitments and the durability of competitive differentiation, but we believe the combination of exceptional growth, emerging earnings capacity, and an attractive entry valuation support a compelling investment opportunity," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note. But the investigations aren’t over Signal joins United Airlines, banks in limiting AI agents over customer risks Amazon faces FAA probe after delivery drone strikes Michigan fiber cable, garage Wedbush analysts initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating and a $120 price target on Monday. They said Anthropic went public in a "tumultuous market" as debate around the AI buildout continues, but that they expect the company to navigate the competitive environment and "capture a uniquely large addressable market." "While there's going to continue to be many ups and downs, and winners and losers as this ecosystem gets built, in our view there is no real question that it does get built over time," the analysts wrote in a Monday note. "The genie is out of the bottle. And ANT is a strong play on that theme." Analysts at Oppenheimer initiated coverage of Anthropic with an outperform rating on Tuesday, and they set a $150 price target for the stock. They said their "bullish stance" on the company stems from their belief that Anthropic will capture growing enterprise AI spending, that its improving compute efficiency lowers cost per task and that its multi-chip strategy optimizes price performance. The analysts added that Anthropic's focus on the enterprise also relies less on consumer subsidies, and that rising customer adoption creates "a substantial runway" for the company. "While competition and compute commitments remain risks, we believe Anthropic can translate its leadership into durable growth and operating leverage," the analysts wrote in a Tuesday note. Michael Kappeler | Picture Alliance | Getty Images Alphabet -owned Waymo said Tuesday its new recall of nearly 4,500 self-driving vehicles in the U.S. was prompted by 11 incidents of robotaxis entering closed freeway lanes since Oct. 1, including three on a single day this month. On Friday, Reuters first reported Waymo was issuing two recalls for its robotaxis over incidents involving closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control. Last week, Waymo said it halted operations of its vehicles on U.S. freeways ​after a California regulator barred its vehicles from freeways in the state. Waymo told the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration in a filing released Tuesday that three Waymo vehicles entered freeway lanes marked with cones as closed for construction on Nov. 9, just three days after the company "updated the approved scope of operation to reduce exposure to closed freeway lanes." Waymo said there were no collisions or injuries reported from the closed freeway events, adding it is still working ​on the recall remedy. The California ban, ​which took effect this month, resulted from a series of incidents in which Waymo robotaxis entered active construction zones, the California Department of Motor Vehicles said. In June, Waymo issued a similar recall for nearly 3,900 robotaxis that drove past ramp closure signs into pre-planned freeway construction zones or entered freeway lanes with active construction by driving between cones. The ‌manual ⁠traffic recall is to ensure self-driving vehicles better respond to manual commands at intersections from law enforcement or other emergency personnel and follows a May 8 collision in which a Waymo followed directions from an officer, but the officer was then temporarily obstructed. That update was completed on Nov. 6. Earlier this month, NHTSA said it opened a recall query into Waymo vehicles after numerous incidents of its robotaxis passing ​stopped school buses. Separately, NHTSA and the ​National Transportation Safety Board have opened probes after one of Waymo's self-driving vehicles struck a child who ran into a street in Santa Monica, California.
